title: When Computers Talk at Once

sources.title: UCSB CS176C: The Shared-Medium Problem
sources.notes: Checked ALOHA vulnerable periods, idealized throughput assumptions, carrier sensing and wired/wireless distinctions.

sources.title: University of Washington CSE461: From Aloha to Ethernet

sources.title: Purdue Networking and Internetworking Lecture Notes

sections.title: One medium, several speakers
sections.narration: Three stations share one communication medium. Watch each transmission occupy the same line. Medium access control answers who may transmit now, rather than which Internet route a packet should follow.
sections.takeaway: Medium access control decides how stations share a communication resource.

sections.title: Make overlap visible
sections.narration: A and C begin before either learns about the other. Their advancing signals overlap, and the frames fail in our shared-medium model. The red disturbance then propagates toward the senders.
bullets: A receiver may lose both frames
sections.takeaway: A collision concerns overlapping signals at a receiver.

sections.title: Pure ALOHA: send when ready
sections.narration: Pure ALOHA sends whenever data is ready. These arrival times have no common slot boundaries. Overlapping frame intervals can collide, requiring a later attempt when success is not confirmed.
sections.takeaway: Pure ALOHA allows a station to begin transmitting whenever data is ready.

sections.title: A vulnerable interval of 2T
sections.narration: For a frame lasting T, interfering starts can occur up to T before or T after its start. The highlighted range spans two T, explaining collisions between slightly offset transmissions.
bullets: Conflicts can start before or after
sections.takeaway: For equal-length pure ALOHA frames, the vulnerable interval spans 2T.

sections.title: Why retry randomly?
sections.narration: Identical retry waits can synchronize another collision. Different waiting times give one station a clearer opportunity while another holds back. Random backoff reduces repeated clashes; it never guarantees the next attempt succeeds.
bullets: Identical waits can repeat a clash
sections.takeaway: Independent retry timing reduces the chance of repeated collisions.

sections.title: Slotted ALOHA adds boundaries
sections.narration: Slotted ALOHA aligns frame starts to a common schedule. These two stations choose the same slot and still collide. A station choosing a different slot avoids that particular overlap.
sections.takeaway: Slotted ALOHA restricts transmission starts to common slot boundaries.

sections.title: The vulnerable interval becomes T
sections.narration: Under the ideal equal-frame slot model, only attempts in the same slot conflict. The vulnerable interval becomes T instead of two T. Synchronization changes the possible collision pattern.
sections.takeaway: Under the ideal slot model, the vulnerable interval is one slot.

sections.title: Interpret the ideal efficiency result
sections.narration: Move along both curves as offered load increases. Under the ideal ALOHA traffic assumptions, pure ALOHA peaks near eighteen-point-four percent; slotted ALOHA peaks near thirty-six-point-eight percent. More attempts eventually reduce useful throughput.
sections.takeaway: The familiar ALOHA maxima depend on a specific ideal traffic model.

sections.title: Scheduling or contention?
sections.narration: A schedule reserves turns. Contention lets stations compete for opportunities. Both must respect the same limited medium. Watch one transmission occupy the line before the other uses that physical resource.
sections.takeaway: Collision reduction comes with assumptions or coordination costs.

sections.title: Listen before transmitting
sections.narration: Carrier sensing distinguishes a locally busy medium from an idle one. A station with data waits while another signal occupies the line, then attempts transmission when its rule permits.
bullets: Defer when the channel is busy
sections.takeaway: Carrier sensing can avoid transmissions that obviously conflict locally.

sections.title: A distant sender can still start
sections.narration: Signals take time to propagate. A distant station may still sense idle just after another starts. Both transmit, their fronts meet, and the collision disturbance travels back toward them.
bullets: Both ends may initially sense idle
sections.takeaway: Propagation delay allows collisions even with carrier sensing.

sections.title: One-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: One-persistent CSMA keeps sensing while the channel is busy. As soon as the local channel becomes idle, the waiting station transmits. Several waiting stations can therefore restart together.
bullets: Transmit when the medium becomes idle
sections.takeaway: One-persistent stations transmit as soon as their sensed channel becomes idle.

sections.title: Nonpersistent CSMA
sections.narration: Nonpersistent CSMA waits a random interval after finding a busy channel, then senses again. The extra gap reduces synchronized attempts, but may leave the medium idle while stations are waiting.
sections.takeaway: Nonpersistent waiting reduces synchronized attempts but can add idle delay.

sections.title: P-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: In an idle slot, p-persistent CSMA transmits with probability p and otherwise defers. Follow the unsuccessful choices before the selected transmission. This version assumes an appropriate slotted decision model.
sections.takeaway: P-persistent CSMA makes a probabilistic choice at an idle slot.

sections.title: Add detection on historical Ethernet
sections.narration: CSMA/CD belongs to shared, half-duplex Ethernet. Stations sense before transmitting and monitor for collisions during transmission. This is not a description of every modern Ethernet link, nor of Wi-Fi.
sections.takeaway: CSMA/CD belongs to shared half-duplex Ethernet, not all modern Ethernet links.

sections.title: Detect, abort, and signal
sections.narration: When a collision is detected, stop the unsuccessful frame and send the required jam behavior before backing off. The moving red disturbance makes the failure known across the shared medium.
sections.takeaway: Collision detection limits time wasted on an already failed transmission.

sections.title: Why propagation affects frame length
sections.narration: A far-end conflict cannot be known instantly. The outgoing signal reaches the far end, and notification returns. Collision detection constrains frame time and network extent: the transmitter must still be transmitting.
bullets: A far-end clash must return in time
sections.takeaway: Collision detection constrains the relation between frame time and network extent.
sections.short_title: The collision must return in time

sections.title: Widen the random retry range
sections.narration: After repeated collisions, the possible random retry choices expand. Watch two choices become four, then eight. Binary exponential backoff spreads contending attempts across a wider range rather than assigning permanent turns.
sections.takeaway: Binary exponential backoff expands the retry-choice range after collisions.

sections.title: Work two retry choices
sections.narration: After the first collision, choose zero or one slot. After the second, choose zero through three. These independent choices produce different waiting intervals, reducing the chance of another simultaneous attempt.
sections.takeaway: After two collisions, this example draws independently from four slot choices.

sections.title: Backoff does not reserve the cable
sections.narration: Finishing a retry delay does not grant ownership. Another station may already occupy the medium. The sender must still follow carrier-sensing rules; its chosen wait is not an exclusive reservation.
sections.takeaway: Finishing a backoff does not guarantee exclusive access.
sections.short_title: Backoff does not reserve a turn

sections.title: Modern switched full duplex
sections.narration: Now replace the shared wire with switched full-duplex links. Separate transmit and receive paths carry opposing flows. This removes the old shared-wire collision scenario, so these links do not use CSMA/CD.
sections.takeaway: Full-duplex switched Ethernet removes the shared-wire collision scenario.

sections.title: Wi-Fi needs different feedback
sections.narration: Wireless stations do not simply perform Ethernet collision detection while transmitting. Watch an access point receive data and return feedback. Avoidance, acknowledgments, and location-dependent sensing shape wireless access behavior.
bullets: Avoidance and ACKs help manage access
sections.takeaway: Wi-Fi uses collision-avoidance mechanisms rather than Ethernet-style CSMA/CD.

sections.title: Compare the added knowledge
sections.narration: ALOHA sends without carrier sensing. CSMA listens before attempting. CSMA/CD also detects shared-wire collisions during transmission. Each adds useful information, but propagation and contention still impose physical limits.
sections.takeaway: Each improvement adds information while retaining physical limitations.

sections.title: Explain the next collision
sections.narration: Follow the next signal and identify its medium first. Ask what stations can sense, how transmission starts are timed, and how retries are chosen. Those rules explain the access behavior you observe.
sections.takeaway: Medium-access behavior depends on both protocol rules and physical context.
